author: haiku
reason: B is easier for a newcomer to follow because it first describes today's page, API and replica, and states the infrastructure rules the design depends on: queue semantics, the 512 MB worker limit, the multipart limits and the bucket lifecycle. It then walks through a simpler flow, with checkpointing left behind a measurement gate, while A starts straight into lease and checkpoint mechanics and assumes context such as "the brief".

author: haiku
reason: Document A is easier for a newcomer to follow because it first explains the current system and the platform rules, including the queue's retry behaviour, the multipart upload limits, the bucket lifecycle rule and each export status, and only then walks through a simpler design that restarts each attempt from the beginning; Document B adds leases, heartbeats and checkpoints, which is more to hold in mind, though its failure table does help.

author: sonnet
reason: A defines the parts of the stack I wouldn't know (the queue's retry and timeout rules, ctx, on_final_failure, and the exact storage and email helper signatures) and holds together as a design, while B has gaps such as file_key being "null until complete" yet used as the upload key in step 8, and no way to get a fresh link from the page.

author: sonnet
reason: B opens by defining the existing pieces a newcomer can't know: the rows API, what the queue guarantees, `ctx`, and the storage and email helpers with their signatures and how they fail. That makes each step readable on its own, while A uses those same helpers and queue behaviours without introducing them, even though A shows its table earlier and adds a short failure summary.

author: haiku
reason: B is a slightly easier read, but A gives the more complete and exact picture. It shows the per-instance key cache as its own part, defines the window by Redis server time, and spells out what the atomic script does step by step. Each step uses the same four headings (starts when, what it does, data kept, if it goes wrong), and it covers Redis failover and the edge cases that B leaves vague or out.

author: haiku
reason: Document B lays out each step the same way: what starts it, what it does, what data it keeps and what happens when it fails. It shows the key cache as its own participant, spells out the Redis script and window key exactly, and covers Redis failover and the extra latency. That gives a newcomer a fuller and more precise picture of how the system works than A's shorter and somewhat looser account. B does mention "the brief" and "requirement 6" without saying what they are.

author: sonnet
reason: B opens with a plain-prose summary of the whole flow (allowed, 429, fail open) before any details, and puts the failure handling in a table that is quick to scan, so a newcomer gets oriented faster; A has more mechanism detail, such as the script steps and failover loss, but it is denser and assumes the reader already has the overall picture.

author: sonnet
reason: B makes the mechanism concrete for a newcomer: it lists the Lua script step by step, shows the Key Service call happening only on a cache miss, and covers more of what can go wrong (Redis failover losing counts, revoked keys staying valid for up to 5 minutes, no circuit breaker), while A's summary and failure table are tidier but explain less of how the system actually works.

author: haiku
reason: B ties the plan to existing code (UserRepository) and explains one copy mechanism up front, an outbox plus a three-step copy rule that works in both directions, with short reasons for its choices, so a newcomer can follow it more easily than A's denser mix of heartbeats, gates, cursors, sweepers and fences.

author: haiku
reason: Document A is built on one mechanism, the outbox plus a single copy rule, which it explains once and then reuses at every step, so a newcomer can hold the whole system in their head. Document B describes more moving parts (heartbeats, gates, three overlapping change paths, two leaders, and both `sot` and `users.source`), and its overview points ahead to step numbers the reader hasn't reached yet.

author: sonnet
reason: B gives a newcomer a mental model before the rollout. It defines source of truth, mirror and a single four-value write mode, then has a separate "How the system runs" section covering writes, deletes, reads, switching and where state lives. A spreads the same mechanics across rollout steps 2, 3 and 9, so the reader has to piece the design together.

author: sonnet
reason: I'd rather be handed B because it opens with what exists today and a five-stage overview, then groups the steps into labelled phases and explains in numbered sub-steps why each mechanism is safe; A has a useful "how the system runs" section, but it is denser and its terms (dual_pg, authority row, the erasure race) give a newcomer less context.

author: haiku
reason: A defines its terms precisely (open period, rollout record, idempotency key) and shows in the diagram and the step list how the rollback route changes with the source mode; B reads more easily at first but is looser and less consistent internally, for example its Reconcile step compares against old-engine invoices that CatchUp only produces later.

author: haiku
reason: A gives a newcomer a clearer overall picture: its diagram covers the whole lifecycle, nesting the rollback steps and including the day-35 no-return and retired states, and its prose is shorter and easier to follow, whereas B is more rigorous but denser, splits rollback into per-mode routes and leaves 14 open questions that make it harder to see how the system works.

author: sonnet
reason: B opens with the idea that keeps billing safe (one idempotency key per customer and period, so a period can never be charged twice), and its diagram shows the blocked rollback path that A leaves to repeated "stay, retry, page" notes. Its numbered rollback steps match the diagram, and its failure table also covers the config service and day 35 cases, so a newcomer can follow the whole system more easily, even though A is more exact about which component enforces the gates.

author: sonnet
reason: A starts with a summary that states the main rule (one idempotency key, so no customer is charged twice), and its diagram, its notes on the diagram, its mode table and its failure table cover the whole lifecycle, including the blocked-rollback path and the locked state, so a newcomer can understand the system quickly; B goes deeper on mechanism (the controller and pending ledger entries) but is harder to follow.

author: haiku
reason: Document A is the one I'd want: its overview names the three possible end states, its terms (open order, outbox, retry job, claim) are defined precisely, and its steps, failure table and per-service storage table cover the cases a newcomer would otherwise have to guess at (retries, the watchdog, late success, re-reserving stock). Document B's summary and failure table are easier to scan, but it skips how reserve and claim calls are retried and leaves vaguer points, such as the refund key and "N tries".

author: haiku
reason: B gives a newcomer a more complete and consistent picture of the system: a table of what each service stores, the open-order and retry-job mechanics, the watchdog and no-record cases, and what the customer sees. A is easier to skim, but it leaves gaps and contradicts itself, for example "Empty cart" in the diagram against "removes confirmed lines only" in step 7.

author: sonnet
reason: A gives a more complete model of the system: a per-service storage table, an explicit order-status lifecycle, precise inbox, outbox and attemptId semantics, and coverage of failure paths that B leaves out (Inventory never answers, a success arriving for an order that is already cancelled, double clicks). B reads a little more easily, with its colour-coded diagram and stated reasons, but A is the one you could reason about the system from.

author: sonnet
reason: A is easier to read, but B gives a newcomer more of the system's shape: a table of what each service stores, the full order status lifecycle, and explicit answers for cases A leaves out, such as Inventory never answering, a success event arriving for an order that was already cancelled, and the race between a claim and the hold expiring.

author: haiku
reason: B gives a newcomer a clear mental model quickly: its summary states the key rule (each row's owner is set at insert and never changes, so a rollback never moves work already in flight), then a short six-step end-to-end flow and one failure table, whereas A's precise detail is dense, front-loads columns before the flow, and refers across two separate 'step N' numberings that are easy to confuse.

author: haiku
reason: B gives a newcomer more grounding: it explains why the move is happening, names the three notification types, says how the broker behaves, lays out both databases' schemas, and describes each component the same way (what starts it, what it does, where its data lives, what happens when it fails), ending with a timeline, while A's end-to-end flow and failure table are tidy but take more of the existing setup for granted.

author: sonnet
reason: Document A explains more to a newcomer: its terms cover how the existing worker, MailRelay, broker and flags actually behave, it gives the message shapes and table columns, it shows how each service loop works (including the lease that keeps a transaction from staying open during the send), and it lists what is still unknown, so it gives a fuller picture of the system, though B's pipeline table is easier to skim.

author: sonnet
reason: B assumes less of the reader: it defines the existing pieces (the caller, the old batch worker, MailRelay, the broker, the outbox). It also gives the message formats, topics and table columns, and it says plainly what is still unknown, so an outsider can piece the whole system together. A's component table is easier to scan, but A leaves more for the reader to infer.
